title: Everyday Math: Fractions and Percentages
subject: Mathematics
description: A small non-programming pack for practicing fraction and percentage fundamentals.

concepts.title: Fractions
concepts.summary: A fraction describes equal parts of a whole; the numerator counts selected parts and the denominator counts total equal parts.

explanations.plain: In a/b, the denominator b tells how many equal parts make the whole, and the numerator a tells how many of those parts are selected.
explanations.worked-example: If a pizza is divided into 8 equal slices and 3 are eaten, the eaten part is 3/8: 3 selected slices out of 8 equal slices.

teachBack.label: the denominator counts equal parts in the whole

concepts.title: Percentages
concepts.summary: A percentage is a number of parts per hundred and can be converted to a decimal by dividing by 100.

explanations.plain: Percent means per hundred. For example, 25% is 25 out of 100, or 0.25 as a decimal.
explanations.worked-example: To find 10% of 80, write 10% as 0.10 and multiply: 0.10 × 80 = 8.

teachBack.label: divide a percent by 100 to get its decimal
multiply the decimal rate by the whole to find the part

misconceptions.title: Numerator and denominator swapped
misconceptions.description: reverses the roles of the selected parts and the total equal parts

explanations.plain: The numerator is the selected-part count on top; the denominator is the total equal-part count on the bottom.

misconceptions.title: Denominators added
misconceptions.description: adds denominators when adding fractions that already have the same denominator

explanations.plain: When denominators match, add the numerators and keep the common denominator.

misconceptions.title: Equivalent fractions missed
misconceptions.description: does not recognize that multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number preserves a fraction's value

explanations.plain: Multiplying both the numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number keeps the fraction equivalent.

misconceptions.title: Percent not converted
misconceptions.description: uses a percent as a whole number rather than converting it to a rate per hundred

explanations.plain: Convert a percent to a decimal by dividing by 100 before multiplying by the whole.

misconceptions.title: Part and whole confused
misconceptions.description: reports the percentage or whole amount instead of the calculated part

explanations.plain: Multiply the decimal rate by the whole to find the part.

misconceptions.title: Discount direction confused
misconceptions.description: adds a discount to the original price rather than subtracting it

explanations.plain: A discount reduces the original price, so subtract the discount amount.

questions.prompt: In the fraction 3/8, what does the 3 count?

options.text: All equal parts in the whole

hints: The numerator is the top number.

fraction-top-bottom-swapped.plain: The 3 is the numerator and counts the selected parts; 8 is the total number of equal parts.

fraction-equivalence-missed.plain: The numerator counts selected parts, not the number of complete wholes.

fraction-add-denominators.plain: The 3 counts how many of the 8 equal parts are selected.

hints: The pieces have the same size, so combine their counts.

fraction-add-denominators.plain: Add the numerators 1 + 2 and keep the common denominator 5, giving 3/5.

fraction-equivalence-missed.plain: Both fractions have denominator 5, so their selected-part counts combine to 3.

fraction-top-bottom-swapped.plain: The denominator remains 5 because all parts are fifths.

hints: Multiply the numerator and denominator by the same number.

fraction-equivalence-missed.plain: Multiplying both parts of 1/2 by 3 gives 3/6, which has the same value.

fraction-top-bottom-swapped.plain: 1/4 is not equal to 1/2; the numerator and denominator must be scaled together.

fraction-add-denominators.plain: 2/3 has a different value; 1/2 becomes 3/6 when both terms are multiplied by 3.

hints: Find one quarter of 20, then take three of those quarters.

fraction-top-bottom-swapped.plain: One quarter of 20 is 5; three quarters is 3 × 5 = 15.

fraction-add-denominators.plain: A fraction of a quantity is found by multiplication: 20 × 3/4 = 15.

hints: Convert both fractions to fifteenths or compare their decimal values.

fraction-top-bottom-swapped.plain: 3/5 is 9/15, while 2/3 is 10/15, so 2/3 is greater.

fraction-equivalence-missed.plain: The fractions are close but not equal: 9/15 is less than 10/15.

fraction-add-denominators.plain: Fractions can be compared using a shared denominator: 3/5 = 9/15 and 2/3 = 10/15.

questions.prompt: What is 25% written as a decimal?
hints: A percent is a number per 100.

percent-not-divided-by-hundred.plain: 25% means 25 out of 100, so divide 25 by 100 to get 0.25.

percent-whole-confused.plain: Move the decimal two places left when converting 25% to a decimal: 0.25.
The part is 0.10 × 80 = 8; 10 is the rate, not the resulting amount.

percent-discount-direction.plain: This asks for the part, not a discounted price: 10% of 80 is 8.

questions.prompt: A $50 item has a 20% discount. What is its price after the discount?
hints: First find 20% of $50, then subtract that amount from $50.

percent-discount-direction.plain: 20% of $50 is $10; a discount subtracts it, so the new price is $50 - $10 = $40.

percent-whole-confused.plain: $10 is the discount amount. The question asks for the price after subtracting it: $40.

percent-not-divided-by-hundred.plain: Use 0.20, not 20: $50 × 0.20 = $10 discount, leaving a $40 price.

percent-whole-confused.plain: 15 is the percent rate; the requested part is 0.15 × 200 = 30.

percent-not-divided-by-hundred.plain: Convert 15% to 0.15, then multiply by 200 to get 30.

percent-discount-direction.plain: This asks for 15% of 200, not 200 reduced by 15; the part is 30.

hints: To convert a decimal to a percent, multiply it by 100.

percent-not-divided-by-hundred.plain: Multiply 0.4 by 100 to convert it to a percent: 40%.

percent-whole-confused.plain: 0.4 is the decimal form; as a percent it is 40%.

percent-discount-direction.plain: 0.4 × 100 = 40, so the equivalent percentage is 40%, not 400%.
